doc.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: What 'fat chords' are: the three sets of four strings
summary: Barker explains playing four-string voicings for volume rather than single-string solos.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: So the basis of just playing a chord would be just playing six . . .
No just playing. Playing chords. You don’t say “just playing.” You say “playing chords.” It’s something that’s a rhythm thing. You do it, and that fills the band. You don’t leave no open spots.
So what do you mean when you say, when you talk about fat playing, fat chords?

Big. You see a guitar has six strings. Four bottom strings, and there’s four in the center, and there’s four at the top. Three elements of fours. [Barker evidently shows the instrument to White.] This is four, right? At the bottom. From here, there’s four in the center. What we got?
You’re talking about six altogether, right?

Yeah. You got four at the bottom. That’s the big strings. E, A, D, G. Now you got A . . . what I said? . . . E, A, D, G. That’s the top four. Big string on top. Then you got D, G, B . . . no. I have to write it down. Calculations. Chords? Fat ones? Whatever?
That’s the E string. E, A, D, G. That’s four. Here’s four. And here’s four. You got what I’m talking about?
You play these four. Then you play these four here. Then you play these four at the bottom. You’re not just playing straight. You’re playing . . . Forget about it. You got that?
O.k. So, in other words, so you . . .

So you playing this four for volume. Then you play them middle four. If you’re going to play a single string, you play these small strings. That’s the E, B, G, D. You play them four. That’s where most of them solo guitars plays on, this little E, because it’s high. You see them rock-and-roll, heavy metal. They get way up the neck. Sound like a clarinet up there, or a flute, piccolo. That’s it. They want something solid, they get here. They want something heavy, rhythm, you play here. So that’s three elements of what you got. You master that. You ain’t going to get none of them virtuosos to be fooling with these others four, sets of four.
No, they don’t. They’re selling. George Benson, you hear him up here. They got that facility. That fast [expletive deleted].
You go down here, bass, you got the volume.
So when you talk about fat chords, what do you mean?
